title: Zero-Shot Learning for Materials Science Texts: Leveraging Duck Typing Principles (MatDuck)

paper.authors: Zhang, Zhang, Yuan, Li (Wuhan University of Technology / Yonsei)
paper.repo: https://github.com/xinzcode/MatDuck (stated in paper Section 'Implementation Details' and in the WanyuGroup/AI-for-Crystal-Materials index) - returns 404 as of 2026-09-04; not archived retrievably (web.archive.org not reachable from this environment); no repo under the author's account (xinzcode) contains MatDuck (repos: BattFailScholar, ClassMATe, DebiasCL, ...)
paper.other_artifacts: Benchmark data = MatSci-NLP (Song, Miret, Liu, ACL 2023; 7 tasks, 8 datasets; public on GitHub BangLab-UdeM-Mila/NLP4MatSci-ACL23 / Hugging Face) - third-party, not the paper's own artifact

dependence.note: MatDuck is a prompting/ICL method whose backbone LLM generates class definitions (Steps 1-3), performs task adaptation and does code-style inference; every reported F1 (Table 2) is LLM output, and the 'GPT-4-Turbo' backbone is one of three live/dead backbones (with Claude 3.5 Sonnet - dead - and LLaMA3-8B - open).

claim.statement: With GPT-4-Turbo as backbone, MatDuck raises zero-shot materials-science text-mining performance from the plain GPT-4 baseline's overall macro-F1 0.557 (micro 0.511) to 0.661 (micro 0.579), a +10.4-point gain averaged over 7 MatSci-NLP tasks (NER 0.497->0.564, RE 0.549->0.579, EAE 0.516->0.538, PC 0.708->0.768, SAR 0.745->0.851, SC 0.354->0.817, SF 0.529->0.516) (Table 2; Section 'Comparison with Zero-Shot Baselines (RQ1)').
claim.metric: Macro-F1 (top row) and micro-F1 (bottom row) per task, classification formulation of MatSci-NLP tasks (Song, Miret, Liu 2023); 'Overall' = mean over the 7 tasks.
claim.original_source: Paper Table 2 (zero-shot and fine-tuning results, macro-F1 top / micro-F1 bottom), Table 1 (dataset statistics), Table 3 (ablations, Claude backbone only). No result files available (repo gone).

protocol.model_status: gpt-4-turbo / gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09: dying, OpenAI shutdown 2026-10-23 (alias stratum: exact snapshot not stated by the paper)
protocol.model_usage_verified: yes as an experimental backbone (Table 2 rows 'GPT-4' and 'MatDuck (GPT4)'), but only the undated alias is given
protocol.prompt_source: not available - prompt templates for class-definition generation (Steps 1-3), fitness counting (Eq. 4-6) and code-style ICL (Figure 3 shows one NER example) were only in the now-missing repository; the paper gives structure (5 properties per class definition, 10% of task texts for adaptation, Python class-style prompt with task constraints as parameters) but not verbatim text
protocol.n_items: not stated whether the full MatSci-NLP evaluation sets were used; Table 1 lists 169,197 samples in total (NER alone 112,191) - the query count formula (Eq. 9) implies one query per sample
protocol.evaluation: Automatic: macro/micro F1 of predicted descriptor class vs gold label per task following Song, Miret, Liu (2023); requires MatSci-NLP evaluation splits and the MatDuck output parser (unavailable).
protocol.environment: unknown (repo unavailable); LLaMA3-8B arm ran on 2x RTX 4090

artifacts.data_public: partial (benchmark data public; the paper's generated class definitions, prompts and predictions are not)
artifacts.data_license: MatSci-NLP: as published by Song et al. 2023 (not verified here); paper artifacts: unknown
artifacts.notes: The AAAI paper and the WanyuGroup index both point to github.com/xinzcode/MatDuck, which no longer exists; the first author's later repo ClassMATe (Active Knowledge Structuring for LLMs in Materials Science Text Mining) is a different method and does not mention MatDuck.

blockers: Paper artifact repository is gone (404): prompt templates, class-definition generation code, task-adaptation code and output parsers are unavailable; the method cannot be re-executed faithfully from the paper text alone.
Model given only as the undated alias 'GPT-4-Turbo' (alias stratum); sampling parameters unreported.

Scale: Table 1 implies up to 169,197 evaluation samples; a full re-run of baseline + MatDuck with gpt-4-turbo pricing would cost several thousand dollars per seed - only a stratified subsample is affordable, and the paper does not state whether it subsampled.
Benchmark data is third-party (MatSci-NLP) and its license was not verified.

baseline_alive.purpose: would be the live baseline if the pipeline could be reconstructed

successors: llama (open weights, hash-pinned; paper's LLaMA3-8B arm)

budget.assumptions: Blocked. For reference: full scale = 169,197 samples x 2 conditions x 3 seeds ~ 1.0M calls x ~700 input tokens ~ 710M tokens ~ $7,100 input alone; a 500-per-task stratified subsample (3,500 items) x 2 conditions x 3 seeds = 21,000 calls ~ $150 plus the class-definition generation overhead (m*h*(1+r)*(1+k) queries, small).

judgment.rule: Not applicable while blocked. If the authors supply the code: survival = MatDuck minus baseline overall macro-F1 difference (paper +0.104) stays positive with a bootstrap 95% CI over items excluding 0 and the same sign on >= 5 of 7 tasks; partial = positive but CI includes 0 or fewer tasks agree; death = difference <= 0.
judgment.notes: SF was the one task where MatDuck slightly hurt GPT-4 (0.529 -> 0.516); SC drove much of the gain (0.354 -> 0.817).

user_checks: Contact the corresponding author (yjl@whut.edu.cn) for the MatDuck code/prompts and the exact GPT-4-Turbo snapshot and evaluation sample sizes? Without them the card stays blocked.
If code is recovered: approve a stratified subsample (e.g. 500 items per task, ~$150 for 3 seeds) instead of the full 169k-sample evaluation?
Census classification: keep as 'alias-only' (GPT-4-Turbo without date) for the H3 snapshot-notation stratum.
domain_notes: MatSci-NLP tasks are descriptor-classification reformulations of NER, relation extraction, event-argument extraction, paragraph/sentence classification, synthesis-action retrieval and slot filling over materials-science abstracts; descriptor meanings vary across tasks (31.6% 'misuse rate'), which is what MatDuck's class-definition anchoring targets. Fine-tuned MatBERT (0.722 macro-F1) still beats all zero-shot variants, so the claim is about zero-shot improvement, not state of the art. Reviewers should note the large sample counts (Table 1) make even 1-point F1 differences statistically significant if the full sets were used.
